title: James

weeks.title: Joy in hard things
weeks.big: Can anything good come out of a bad week?
context: James was one of Jesus's younger brothers. Growing up, he didn't believe Jesus was the Messiah (John 7:5). Then the risen Jesus appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7) and everything changed. Notice how he introduces himself: not 'the brother of Jesus' but 'a servant'.
He writes to believers scattered far from home, many of them poor and pushed around by powerful people. Life was hard. That's exactly where James starts.

Our translation says 'temptations' in verse 2. The Greek word (peirasmos) means any test or hard thing that puts you under pressure, so most translations say 'trials' here. James uses the same word in two ways: a trial that grows you, or a temptation that trips you. Next week he picks up the second meaning.
words: Scattered abroad: God's people living away from their homeland.
Keeping going while carrying a heavy load.
Complete, fully grown, mature. Not 'never making mistakes'.
Without telling you off or making you feel stupid for asking.
Two minds pulling in opposite directions: trusting God and not trusting him at the same time.
notice: How does James tell them to feel about hard times? Is that what you'd expect?
Find the chain: testing produces … which leads to …
What should you do if you don't know what to do?

dig.q: James doesn't say trials ARE joy. He says COUNT them as joy. What's the difference?
dig.a: Counting is a decision, not a feeling. We don't pretend hard things are nice. We decide to look at them in the light of what God is doing through them. The joy is in where they lead.

dig.q: Why would testing produce endurance? Think about how muscles grow.
dig.a: Muscles only grow when they're put under load. Faith is the same: it gets strong when it has to hold weight. A faith that's never tested stays weak.

dig.q: Why does James jump from trials (verses 2–4) straight to wisdom (verse 5)?
dig.a: Because in hard times the thing we need most is to know what to do and how to see it. God doesn't promise to remove every trial, but he does promise wisdom, generously, and without telling us off for asking.

dig.q: What is a double-minded person like? Why the picture of a wave?
dig.a: Someone who asks God but half-expects him not to help, and keeps a back-up plan that doesn't need him. A wave has no anchor: it goes wherever the wind pushes. James wants us anchored in trusting God.

weeks.young: Can you think of something you had to keep practising until you could do it (riding a bike, swimming, reading)? How did it feel at the end?
weeks.principle: God uses hard things to grow us, and he gladly gives wisdom to anyone who asks.
weeks.why: Our natural question in trouble is 'How do I get out of this?' James teaches a better one: 'What is God growing in me through this, and what is the wise thing to do?'
passage: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion: Greetings.
Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations,
knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
But let him ask in faith, without any doubting, for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven by the wind and tossed.
For that man shouldn’t think that he will receive anything from the Lord.
He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

jesus.text: “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
jesus.note: Jesus told his followers to rejoice when they were treated badly for his sake. James had heard it first-hand.

also.text: Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope:
also.note: Paul describes the same chain: suffering, then perseverance, then character, then hope.

also.text: Give your servant therefore an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil; for who is able to judge this great people of yours?”
also.note: Solomon could have asked for anything. He asked for wisdom, and God was delighted.

scenarios: A test or match goes badly.
A friend leaves you out.
Something you were looking forward to is cancelled.
Someone in the family is ill.
tryThis: Each evening, share one hard thing from the day and ask: 'What might God be growing in us through this?'
When anyone doesn't know what to do, stop and ask God for wisdom together, right then.
Write one hard thing on the fridge card now. Come back to it on Check-in day.
weeks.pray: Each person names one real situation where they need wisdom this week. Ask God for it, trusting him to give generously.

anchor.text: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.

stretch.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

weeks.title: Where temptation comes from
weeks.big: When I do wrong, whose fault is it?
context: Verses 9–11 speak to rich and poor in the scattered church. A poor believer has a high position in God's family. A rich one should remember that money fades like a wildflower in the hot sun. The 'scorching wind' was the sirocco, a burning desert wind that could wither a field in a day.
In verse 12 the word means a trial you endure. In verses 13–14 it shifts to temptation to do wrong. The same hard situation can be a test that grows you or a temptation that trips you.
'Father of lights' means God made the sun, moon and stars. But lights in the sky change: they rise and set and cast moving shadows. God never changes. His goodness doesn't flicker.
words: Poor; low down in how the world sees you.
The prize of life with God, like the wreath a winning athlete received.
Strong desire for something wrong (not only about bodies; any greedy wanting).
When a baby begins to grow. James uses birth as a picture of how sin grows.
The first and best of the harvest, given to God.
notice: Who does James say does NOT tempt us?
Find the chain in verses 14–15: desire → … → …
Where does every good gift come from?

dig.q: Why do we blame God or other people when we do wrong? Can you think of the first time it happened in the Bible?
dig.a: It's as old as Eden. Adam blamed Eve and even God ('the woman you gave me'); Eve blamed the serpent (Genesis 3:12–13). Blaming feels safer than owning it. James says the source is inside us: our own desires.

dig.q: James describes sin like a baby growing: conceived, born, full grown. What's the point of the picture?
dig.a: Sin starts small and hidden, as a desire we keep feeding. Given time it grows into actions, then habits, then destruction. The best time to deal with it is while it's small: at the wanting stage.

dig.q: Verse 16 says 'Don't be deceived.' What lie might we believe about God when we're tempted or when life goes wrong?
dig.a: That God is trying to trip us up, or holding back good things. James says the opposite: everything good comes from him, and he never changes. So when we're tempted, we run to God, not away from him.

dig.q: How do verses 9–11 (rich and poor) fit a passage about testing?
dig.a: Both poverty and riches test us. Poverty tempts us to think we're worthless. Riches tempt us to think we're safe without God. Both people need to see themselves the way God sees them.

weeks.young: Name three good gifts from God you've enjoyed today.
weeks.principle: Temptation grows from our own desires, so own your choices; and every good thing comes from a God who never changes.
weeks.why: If we blame others, we never change. If we see God as the giver of everything good, we run to him when we're tempted instead of hiding from him.
passage: But let the brother in humble circumstances glory in his high position;
and the rich, in that he is made humble, because like the flower in the grass, he will pass away.
For the sun arises with the scorching wind and withers the grass, and the flower in it falls, and the beauty of its appearance perishes. So the rich man will also fade away in his pursuits.
Blessed is a person who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to those who love him.
Let no man say when he is tempted, “I am tempted by God,” for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.
But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.
Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.
Don’t be deceived, my beloved brothers.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.
Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.

jesus.text: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
jesus.note: Jesus said that if imperfect parents give good things to their children, our Father in heaven gives far better.

also.text: The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
also.note: God always provides a way out of temptation.

scenarios: You snap at your brother or sister and want to say 'they started it'.
You want something that isn't yours: a toy, a turn, someone else's praise.
You're tempted to do something online you know you shouldn't.
tryThis: Practise owning it: when something goes wrong, say 'I chose to…' instead of 'They made me…'
Keep a 'good gifts' list on the fridge. Everyone adds one thing each day.
Spot a temptation early: each person names one 'small desire' they will starve this week.
weeks.pray: Thank God for three specific good gifts each. Then ask for help with one temptation.

anchor.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.

stretch.text: Blessed is a person who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to those who love him.

weeks.title: Don't just listen. Do it.
weeks.big: What's the point of hearing something if nothing changes?
context: Christians in James's day mostly heard Scripture rather than read it. Few people owned a copy; it was read aloud when the church met. So a 'hearer' was someone who sat and listened, nodded along, and went home unchanged.
Mirrors were polished bronze: a dim, wobbly reflection. You glanced, then forgot. James says hearing God's word without doing it is like that glance: you saw yourself, but nothing happened.
In that world, orphans and widows had no one to provide for them: no pensions, no benefits. Caring for them was costly and practical. That, says James, is what real religion looks like.
This is the key verse for the whole of Bible Lab. We're not here to collect verses but to live them.
words: Planted inside you, like a seed.
God's word, which sets us free instead of tying us up.
The straps used to steer a horse.
Not soaked through with the world's ways of thinking and living.
notice: What three things should we be quick or slow at (verse 19)?
What happens to the man with the mirror?
What does pure religion look like (verse 27)?

dig.q: Why does James say hearing without doing is deceiving YOURSELF?
dig.a: Because hearing feels like progress. You understand it, you agree, you feel good, so you think you've changed. But nothing in your life is different. The danger isn't fooling others; it's fooling ourselves.

dig.q: Why does 'quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger' come right before 'receive the word'?
dig.a: A heart that's busy talking and angry can't hear God. Listening well to people and listening well to God go together. Anger closes the ears.

dig.q: What's the difference between the glance in the mirror and 'looking into the law and continuing'?
dig.a: The second is a long, careful look that keeps going: you come back, you remember, you act. That's what we're doing in Bible Lab: a long look at a small passage, all week.

dig.q: James's test of real religion is: your tongue, care for the vulnerable, and purity. Why those three?
dig.a: All three are visible. They're about what you say, who you help and how you live, not how religious you sound. They're also exactly what James talks about in the rest of the letter.

weeks.young: If you only listened to your swimming teacher but never got in the pool, could you swim?
weeks.principle: God's word is meant to be done, not just heard. Hearing without doing fools ourselves.
weeks.why: This is the hinge of the letter and of this whole lab. Every week the question isn't 'Did we understand it?' but 'What are we doing about it?'
passage: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.
Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

jesus.text: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.”
jesus.note: Jesus finished his greatest sermon with this story. The difference between the two builders isn't hearing: both heard. It's doing.

also.text: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.

scenarios: An argument is starting and you have something clever to say.
Someone at school or church is lonely or left out.
You've just heard a great talk or lesson. What now?
tryThis: Listening rule at meals: before you answer anyone, say back what they said.
As a family, do one practical thing for someone who is alone or struggling: a card, a visit, a meal.
At the end of every session this week, each person says one thing they will actually do.
weeks.pray: Pray for someone you know who is lonely or struggling. Ask God to show you how to help them, then do it.

anchor.text: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.

stretch.text: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;

weeks.title: No favourites
weeks.big: Do we treat some people as if they matter more?
context: Seating showed status. The best seats went to important people. Rich visitors could bring money, protection and connections, so making a fuss of them was completely normal in that culture.

But most of James's readers were poor, and it was rich landowners who were dragging them to court and exploiting them (verse 6). Bowing to the rich while pushing the poor aside was unfair and upside down.
'The royal law' is 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus called it the second greatest commandment. It's royal because it's the King's law and it rules over all the others.
words: Favouritism: treating people differently because of how they look or what they have.
Meeting place. Many early Christians still met in one.
Kindness to someone who doesn't deserve it.
notice: Describe the two people who walk in. How is each treated?
Who has God chosen to be rich in faith?
What 'triumphs over judgment'?

dig.q: Why is favouritism such a big deal to James? It's only seats!
dig.a: Because it shows what we really value. Favouritism treats people by how useful or impressive they are, not by their worth to God. Every person is made in God's image, and God himself chose the poor and overlooked.

dig.q: Verse 10 says breaking one law makes you guilty of all. Isn't that harsh?
dig.a: God's law is one whole thing, like a window: crack it anywhere and the window is broken. James is stopping people from thinking 'I'm fine because I don't do the big sins.' Favouritism isn't small just because respectable people do it.

dig.q: Who might be the 'poor man in filthy clothing' in our world? In our house?
dig.a: The new kid, the awkward one, someone with a disability, someone poorer or from a different background, the unpopular one. At home: who gets our attention, and who gets ignored?

dig.q: What does 'mercy triumphs over judgment' mean?
dig.a: People who have received God's mercy should be merciful. If we judge others harshly by appearances, we've forgotten how much mercy we've been shown. Mercy wins.

weeks.young: If two children came to play, one with a brilliant toy and one with nothing, who would you want to play with? What would Jesus do?
weeks.principle: Every person has equal worth to God, so love without favourites.
weeks.why: Favouritism is everywhere: popularity, looks, money, talent. Followers of Jesus are called to notice the people everyone else overlooks.
passage: My brothers, don’t hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with partiality.
For if a man with a gold ring, in fine clothing, comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in filthy clothing also comes in,
and you pay special attention to him who wears the fine clothing and say, “Sit here in a good place;” and you tell the poor man, “Stand there,” or “Sit by my footstool”
haven’t you shown partiality among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?
Listen, my beloved brothers. Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom which he promised to those who love him?
But you have dishonored the poor man. Don’t the rich oppress you, and personally drag you before the courts?
Don’t they blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called?
However, if you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well.
But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.
For whoever keeps the whole law, and yet stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all.
For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not commit murder.” Now if you do not commit adultery, but murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
So speak and so do, as men who are to be judged by a law of freedom.
For judgment is without mercy to him who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

jesus.text: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back. But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”
jesus.note: Jesus told a host to invite the people who could never pay him back.

also.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
also.note: People look at the outside; God looks at the heart.

also.text: Jesus said to him, “ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
also.note: The royal law, in Jesus's words.

scenarios: Choosing teams in PE.
A new kid sits alone at lunch.
A visitor nobody knows comes to church.
tryThis: Each person notices one 'overlooked' person this week and does something kind for them.
No favourites at home: notice who always gets the best seat, the last word or the most attention, and switch it.
Sit with someone different at church or at lunch.
weeks.pray: Ask God to help you see people the way he sees them. Pray by name for someone who is often left out.

anchor.text: However, if you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well.

stretch.text: For judgment is without mercy to him who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

weeks.title: Faith that works
weeks.big: Can you have real faith that doesn't change anything?
context: Some people thought believing the right things was enough, whether or not it changed how they lived. James answers with a blunt example: telling a hungry person 'Keep warm and eat well!' and giving them nothing.

Is James arguing with Paul? Paul says we're saved by faith, not works (Ephesians 2:8–9). James says faith without works is dead. They're fighting different problems. Paul is against trying to earn God's love; James is against fake faith that never shows. Paul's very next sentence agrees with James: we are created 'for good works' (Ephesians 2:10). We are saved by faith alone, but saving faith is never alone.

James's two examples are as different as possible: Abraham, the respected father of the nation (Genesis 22), and Rahab, a foreign woman with a bad reputation (Joshua 2). Both showed they trusted God by what they did when it was costly.
words: Shown to be right with God.
The Shema, the most basic Jewish statement of belief, said every day.
notice: What does the person in verse 16 say? What do they actually do?
Who else believes 'God is one' (verse 19)?
Who are James's two examples?

dig.q: Why mention that demons believe God is one?
dig.a: Because simply agreeing with facts isn't the faith James means. Demons know the facts perfectly. Real faith is trust, and trust always shows in what you do.

dig.q: How did Abraham's action show his faith?
dig.a: He trusted God enough to be willing to give up the son God had promised him, believing God would keep his promise anyway (Hebrews 11:19). His action didn't earn God's trust; it showed his trust was real.

dig.q: Why Rahab, of all people?
dig.a: To show this isn't just for spiritual heroes. Rahab was an outsider with a bad past, but she risked her life to protect God's people because she believed God was real. Anyone can have faith that acts.

dig.q: Paul says 'not by works'. James says 'faith without works is dead'. How can both be true?
dig.a: Think of a tree: faith is the roots, works are the fruit. The fruit doesn't make the tree alive, but a living tree will grow fruit. Works are the evidence of faith, not the cause of salvation.

weeks.young: If I said I loved you but never hugged you, helped you or spent time with you, how would you know I meant it?
weeks.principle: Real faith always shows up in what we do. We are saved by faith alone, but faith is never alone.
weeks.why: This guards us from two mistakes: trying to earn God's love, and claiming a faith that never costs us anything.
passage: What good is it, my brothers, if a man says he has faith, but has no works? Can faith save him?
And if a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food,
and one of you tells them, “Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;” yet you didn’t give them the things the body needs, what good is it?
Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.
Yes, a man will say, “You have faith, and I have works.” Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works.
You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe, and shudder.
But do you want to know, vain man, that faith apart from works is dead?
Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?
You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected.
So the Scripture was fulfilled which says, “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness,” and he was called the friend of God.
You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith.
In the same way, wasn’t Rahab the prostitute also justified by works, in that she received the messengers and sent them out another way?
For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.

jesus.text: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.
jesus.note: Saying the right words isn't the same as doing the Father's will.

also.text: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
also.note: Paul: saved by grace, through faith, for good works.

scenarios: A friend is having a hard time and you say 'I'll pray for you'.
There's a food bank collection at school or church.
Someone needs help and you're busy.
tryThis: Turn one 'I'll pray for you' into a prayer AND an action this week.
As a family, give something practical: a food bank bag, a meal for someone, clothes you no longer need.
Each person asks: 'Where would someone see my faith in my week?'
weeks.pray: Pray that your faith would show in your hands and feet. Pray for someone who needs practical help, and decide what you'll do.

anchor.text: Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.

stretch.text: For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.

weeks.title: Small but powerful
weeks.big: Can words really do as much damage as actions?
context: Teachers in the early church had huge influence, and teaching is mostly talking. So James starts there: anyone who speaks a lot carries more responsibility for what they say.

James uses pictures his readers knew: a small bit steering a strong horse, a small rudder turning a big ship in a gale, a spark setting a dry hillside on fire. Wildfires were common in the hot, dry summers around Israel.
'Gehenna' was a valley outside Jerusalem where rubbish was burned, and it became a picture of hell. James is saying cruel words have their source in evil itself.
words: The metal piece in a horse's mouth used to steer it.
The small blade at the back of a ship that steers it.
The burning rubbish valley outside Jerusalem; a picture of hell.
Every person reflects God, so speaking against them is serious.
notice: Find the three pictures of small things that control or destroy big things.
What can people tame? What can't they?
What two things come out of the same mouth?

dig.q: Why is the tongue like a rudder? Like a fire?
dig.a: Rudder: your words set the direction of your life and relationships. Fire: one spiteful comment, rumour or message can spread far beyond what you meant, and it can't be taken back.

dig.q: James says no one can tame the tongue. Is that hopeless?
dig.a: No human can do it by willpower alone. That's why we need God. Jesus said words come from the heart (Matthew 12:34), so God changes our words by changing our hearts.

dig.q: Why is it so wrong to praise God and then speak badly about a person?
dig.a: Because that person is made in God's image. It's like praising an artist and then slashing their painting. How we talk about people shows what we really think of God.

dig.q: How does this apply to messages, group chats and posts?
dig.a: Typing is still the tongue. Online it's often worse: faster, wider, permanent, and easier to be cruel when you can't see someone's face.

weeks.young: Squeeze some toothpaste out of the tube. Now try to put it back in. What does that teach us about words?
weeks.principle: Words have huge power to build up or tear down, and they show what's in our heart.
weeks.why: Most of the wrong we do in a day is probably spoken. A family that changes how it speaks to each other changes everything.
passage: Let not many of you be teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive heavier judgment.
For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.
Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature, is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?
Can a fig tree, my brothers, yield olives, or a vine figs? Thus no spring yields both salt water and fresh water.

jesus.text: You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things. I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”
jesus.note: Jesus: the mouth speaks what fills the heart.

also.text: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.
also.note: Life and death are in the power of the tongue.

also.text: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
also.note: Only words that build others up.

scenarios: Your sibling messes up and you want to mock them.
Someone in the group chat starts making fun of someone.
You're frustrated and want to say something sharp.
tryThis: Toothpaste challenge: leave a tube on the table all week as a reminder.
Family rule: every unkind word must be followed by an apology and two kind ones.
Each day, encourage one person by name, with a specific reason.
weeks.pray: Ask God to make your mouth a spring of fresh water this week. Say sorry for any words that have hurt someone in the family.

anchor.text: Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

stretch.text: So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!

weeks.title: Two kinds of wisdom
weeks.big: How can you tell if someone is truly wise?
context: In the ancient world 'wise' people were known for clever speeches and winning arguments. Teachers competed for followers. James says real wisdom shows in how you live, especially in how gently you treat people.
Earthly wisdom is driven by 'bitter jealousy and selfish ambition': looking out for number one. It can look smart and successful but leaves a mess behind.
Wisdom 'from above' sounds a lot like the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), and a lot like Jesus. Read verse 17 again and put Jesus's name in.
words: Wanting to get ahead, whatever it costs other people.
Driven by natural instincts instead of by God.
Willing to listen and give way.
notice: How does a wise person show their wisdom (verse 13)?
What two things cause confusion and evil (verse 16)?
Count the qualities of wisdom from above (verse 17).

dig.q: James says wisdom shows in gentleness. We often think clever people are sharp. Why gentle?
dig.a: Real wisdom isn't about winning; it's about doing good. Gentleness is strength under control. A wise person can be right without being cruel.

dig.q: How do jealousy and selfish ambition cause 'confusion and every evil deed'?
dig.a: When everyone's trying to get ahead, teams split, friends compete, families argue. Selfish ambition always needs someone else to lose.

dig.q: Which quality in verse 17 do you find hardest? Which does our family most need?
dig.a: No right answer: let everyone share honestly. 'Reasonable' (willing to give way) is hard for most of us!

dig.q: What does verse 18 mean by sowing peace?
dig.a: Peacemakers are like farmers: every peaceful word or act is a seed. Over time they reap a harvest of right living. Peace isn't passive; you have to plant it.

weeks.young: Is it wiser to win an argument, or to be friends again? Why?
weeks.principle: True wisdom from God shows in a pure, peaceful, gentle life, not in being clever or getting ahead.
weeks.why: We're surrounded by 'wisdom' that says look after yourself first. God's wisdom builds peace instead.
passage: Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.
But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth.
This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.
For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

jesus.text: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
jesus.note: Jesus called peacemakers blessed: true children of God.

also.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
also.note: The fruit of the Spirit: the same family likeness.

also.text: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

scenarios: A group project where you want the credit.
You're jealous of a friend's success.
Two people are arguing and you could take sides or make peace.
tryThis: Peacemaker of the day: at dinner, each person names someone who made peace today.
Celebrate someone else's success out loud this week, especially if you're jealous of it.
In one disagreement this week, choose to give way gently.
weeks.pray: Read verse 17 together. Each person picks one quality and asks God to grow it in them.

anchor.text: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.

stretch.text: Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

weeks.title: Fights, pride and drawing near
weeks.big: Where do our fights come from?
context: The churches James wrote to were full of quarrels: rich against poor, teachers competing, people speaking against each other. James goes beneath the surface to the root.
'Adulterers' (verse 4) is an Old Testament picture. God's people are like a bride; loving the world's values instead of God is like being unfaithful in a marriage.
Verse 6 quotes Proverbs 3:34. Pride says 'I don't need God or anyone'. Humility says 'I need God'. God resists the first and pours grace on the second.
words: Want what belongs to someone else.
Sharing the world's values and priorities (not enjoying God's creation).
Honest about how much we need God.
Criticise or run someone down, usually behind their back.
notice: Where do fights come from, according to verse 1?
List the commands in verses 7–10.
What does God do if we draw near to him?

dig.q: Think of the last argument in our house. What did each person want?
dig.a: Let people answer honestly. Usually it's control, attention, a turn, to be right, or comfort. The fight outside starts with a fight inside.

dig.q: Verse 2: 'You don't have, because you don't ask.' Verse 3: some ask with wrong motives. What's the difference?
dig.a: Some of us grab instead of asking God. Others ask God, but only to get what we want for ourselves. God loves to give; he wants us to ask with hearts that want what he wants.

dig.q: What does it mean to 'draw near to God'?
dig.a: Turning towards him: praying, reading his word, saying sorry, trusting him. And the promise is wonderful: he draws near too. He isn't far away waiting for us to be good enough.

dig.q: Why does James say speaking against each other is 'judging the law'?
dig.a: God's law says love your neighbour. When we run people down, we act as if we're above that law, setting ourselves up as judge. Only God is judge.

weeks.young: When two people both want the same toy, what's going on inside them? What could they do instead of fighting?
weeks.principle: Fights start with selfish desires inside us. The way out is to humble ourselves and draw near to God.
weeks.why: It's easy to blame the other person in a fight. James asks us to look at our own hearts first, and promises that God gives grace to the humble.
passage: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge.
Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?

jesus.text: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye;’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.
jesus.note: Jesus: deal with the plank in your own eye before the speck in someone else's.

also.text: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
also.note: Peter says the same thing as James 4:10.

scenarios: Two siblings arguing over the remote, a seat or a turn.
You run someone down behind their back.
You want to win more than you want to be kind.
tryThis: In a fight this week, ask yourself 'What do I want right now?' before you say anything.
Say sorry first, even if you think it's 50/50.
Talk to God about someone before you talk about them.
weeks.pray: Draw near: two minutes of quiet together, then each person says one honest sentence to God.

anchor.text: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

stretch.text: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.

weeks.title: If the Lord wills
weeks.big: Who's really in charge of tomorrow?
context: Merchants in the Roman world travelled from city to city trading goods. James pictures a businessman with a confident plan: which city, how long, how much profit. Planning isn't wrong. Planning as if God weren't there is.
A 'vapour' is like your breath on a cold morning or mist over a field: here, then gone. James says this not to scare us but to wake us up.

In 5:1–6 James speaks to rich landowners who were cheating their farm workers. Labourers were paid at the end of each day (Leviticus 19:13); holding back wages meant their families went hungry that night. God hears their cries.
words: Mist or steam: visible for a moment, then gone.
God as commander of heaven's armies: he will defend the poor.
notice: What is the merchant planning?
What does James say we should say instead?
Find the three things that have rotted or rusted in 5:2–3.

dig.q: Is James against making plans?
dig.a: No. He's against plans that leave God out, as if we control tomorrow. 'If the Lord wills' isn't a magic phrase; it's an attitude: holding our plans with open hands.

dig.q: Why does James call our life a vapour? Is that depressing?
dig.a: It's honest, and it's freeing. It helps us stop wasting time and focus on what matters. A short life plus God in charge means: live for what lasts.

dig.q: 4:17 says knowing the good thing and not doing it is sin. How does that link to week 3?
dig.a: Same theme: doing, not just knowing. Sin isn't only doing wrong things; it's also leaving undone the good we know we should do.

dig.q: What was wrong with the rich people in 5:1–6?
dig.a: They hoarded wealth that rotted, lived in luxury, and got rich by cheating their workers. Wealth isn't evil, but hoarding it and gaining it unfairly is. God hears the people who are cheated.

weeks.young: Breathe on a cold window or a mirror and watch the mist disappear. What does James say is like that?
weeks.principle: Hold your plans and possessions loosely: life is short and God is in charge, so do the good you know to do now.
weeks.why: We all live as if tomorrow is guaranteed. Remembering that God holds tomorrow makes us humble and makes us generous.
passage: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.”
Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away.
For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.”
But now you glory in your boasting. All such boasting is evil.
To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.
Come now, you rich, weep and howl for your miseries that are coming on you.
Your riches are corrupted and your garments are moth-eaten.
Your gold and your silver are corroded, and their corrosion will be for a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up your treasure in the last days.
Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies.
You have lived in luxury on the earth, and taken your pleasure. You have nourished your hearts as in a day of slaughter.
You have condemned and you have murdered the righteous one. He doesn’t resist you.

jesus.text: He spoke a parable to them, saying, “The ground of a certain rich man produced abundantly. He reasoned within himself, saying, ‘What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?’ He said, ‘This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. I will tell my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.” ’ “But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’ So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
jesus.note: Jesus told the story of a rich man with big plans and bigger barns.

also.text: Don’t boast about tomorrow; for you don’t know what a day may bring.

“Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
also.note: Treasure that moths and rust can't touch.

scenarios: Planning the holidays, a birthday or next week.
You know you should help with something but keep putting it off.
You're saving up for something and can't stop thinking about it.
tryThis: Plan the family week together, then pray over the plans: 'If the Lord wills…'
Each person does one good thing they've been putting off.
Give away something you're hoarding: money, toys or time.
weeks.pray: Bring your plans for this week to God and ask him to lead them. Thank him for today.

anchor.text: To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.

stretch.text: Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away. For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.”

weeks.title: Patient and true
weeks.big: How do you keep going when waiting is hard?
context: Farmers in Israel sowed seed and then depended on two rains: the early rain in autumn to soften the ground, and the late rain in spring to swell the crop. After sowing there was nothing to do but wait and trust.
James's readers were waiting for Jesus to return and put things right, while being treated unfairly. Patience here isn't sitting still; it's staying faithful while you wait.
People swore oaths ('I swear by heaven!') to make promises sound extra serious. But that suggested their normal words couldn't be trusted. Jesus taught the same thing (Matthew 5:37).
words: Able to wait without giving up or complaining.
Make your hearts strong and steady.
Swearing by something to make your words sound more true.
notice: Who is our example of patience in verse 7?
Whose stories does James point to in verses 10–11?
What should our 'yes' and 'no' be like?

dig.q: Why is a farmer a good picture of patience?
dig.a: A farmer does his part (ploughing, sowing), then waits for what only God can do (rain, growth). He doesn't dig up the seeds every day to check! Patience is trusting God with the part we can't control.

dig.q: Why does James mention grumbling here?
dig.a: When we're waiting and under pressure, we turn on each other. Grumbling is impatience aimed at people. Families under pressure grumble at each other most.

dig.q: What do we learn from Job?
dig.a: Job lost almost everything and had hard questions, but he didn't let go of God. In the end we see 'the Lord is full of compassion and mercy'. Endurance trusts that God's ending will be good, even when we can't see it yet.

dig.q: What does it look like to let your yes be yes?
dig.a: Being someone whose word is enough: you do what you said, you turn up, you tell the truth without needing to swear. Trustworthiness.

weeks.young: Have you ever planted a seed? What would happen if you dug it up every day to check on it?
weeks.principle: Wait for God patiently, without grumbling, and be someone whose word can be trusted.
weeks.why: Patience and trustworthiness are quiet things, but they hold families and friendships together.
passage: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged. Behold, the judge stands at the door.
Take, brothers, for an example of suffering and of perseverance, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job, and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
But above all things, my brothers, don’t swear— not by heaven, or by the earth, or by any other oath; but let your “yes” be “yes”, and your “no”, “no”, so that you don’t fall into hypocrisy.

jesus.text: But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.
jesus.note: James's 'yes be yes' is almost word for word what his brother taught.

also.text: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.
He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name.”
also.note: Job's response when he lost everything.

scenarios: Waiting for something you really want: a birthday, a result, a friend to change.
You promised to do something and don't feel like it now.
Everyone's tired and starting to snap.
tryThis: No-grumble day: pick one day with no complaining, and catch each other kindly.
Keep every small promise this week, even 'I'll be there in a minute'.
Plant a seed together as a reminder to wait well.
weeks.pray: Each person names something they're waiting for, and hands it to God.

anchor.text: You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.

stretch.text: But above all things, my brothers, don’t swear— not by heaven, or by the earth, or by any other oath; but let your “yes” be “yes”, and your “no”, “no”, so that you don’t fall into hypocrisy.

weeks.title: Pray about everything
weeks.big: What should we do with every situation in life?
context: James ends not with a summary but with prayer. Whatever is happening (suffering, joy, sickness, sin) the answer starts with talking to God.

Oil was used in the ancient world as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God. Christians understand verse 14 in different ways, but the clear point is that the church should pray for the sick, and healing is in God's hands.

Elijah's story is in 1 Kings 17–18: he prayed and there was no rain for three and a half years; he prayed again and the rain came. James's point is that Elijah was 'a man with a nature like ours'. Ordinary people's prayers matter.
words: Pour or rub oil on someone.
Right with God; living God's way.
notice: What should you do if you're suffering? Cheerful? Sick?
What two things should we do for one another (verse 16)?
Who is James's example of prayer?

dig.q: Why does James say to pray in suffering AND in happy times?
dig.a: Because God isn't only for emergencies. Calling on him in hard times and praising him in good times means our whole life is lived with him.

dig.q: Why confess to one another, and not only to God?
dig.a: Hidden wrongs break relationships. Saying them out loud to someone you trust brings things into the light, and then they can pray for you. In a family it sounds like 'I was wrong, I'm sorry' and 'I forgive you'.

dig.q: Why does James point out that Elijah was 'like us'?
dig.a: So we don't think prayer only works for super-spiritual people. God listens to ordinary people who trust him.

dig.q: Why end the whole letter with turning back someone who wanders?
dig.a: The whole letter is about faith that's real. If someone drifts, the loving thing is to go after them gently. James ends with caring for each other.

weeks.young: Do you only talk to your friends when you need something? How should we talk to God?
weeks.principle: Bring everything to God in prayer, and help each other stay close to him.
weeks.why: If James is about faith that works, prayer is where it starts: faith that talks to God, in good times and bad.
passage: Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises.
Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord,
and the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.
Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it didn’t rain on the earth for three years and six months.
He prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.
Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back,
let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.

jesus.text: Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”
jesus.note: Jesus promised to be there when even two or three gather in his name: a family praying together.

also.text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
also.note: Pray about everything instead of worrying.

also.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

scenarios: Someone in the family is ill.
You did something wrong and nobody knows.
A really good thing happens.
tryThis: Start a family prayer list on the fridge: add requests and tick off answers.
Say sorry and forgive before bed: no going to sleep on a quarrel.
Each person prays out loud for the person on their left, at least once this week.
weeks.pray: Pray for each other by name, one by one round the table.

anchor.text: Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

stretch.text: Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises.

weeks.title: Review: faith that works
weeks.big: What has actually changed in us?
context: Twelve weeks ago we started with one question: what does real faith look like? James's answer, in one line: real faith shows up in real life.

This week, read the whole letter aloud in one sitting. It takes about 15 minutes. Take turns, a paragraph each. You'll hear every passage you've studied, now joined up, and notice how the themes keep coming back: trials, wisdom, words, rich and poor, humility, doing.
notice: Which passage sounded different now that you know it well?
Which themes kept coming back again and again?
What does James say most often?

dig.q: If you had to sum up James in one sentence, what would it be?
dig.a: Something like: 'Real faith shows up in real life.' Or James 1:22: be doers of the word, not only hearers.

dig.q: Which principle has made the biggest difference to you? Which has been hardest?
dig.a: No right answer. Let everyone share, grown-ups included.

dig.q: Where have we seen our family change in these twelve weeks?
dig.a: Look back at the 'This week we will' list. Celebrate what has stuck, without guilt about what hasn't.

weeks.young: Which week's activity did you like best: the toothpaste, the mist on the window, the seed?
weeks.principle: Real faith shows up in real life.
weeks.why: We didn't do this to finish a book. We did it so James would live in us: in our words, our fights, our plans and our prayers.

jesus.text: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.”
jesus.note: Where we began: the wise builder hears and does.

tryThis: Choose two 'This week we will' habits to keep as family habits.
Have a celebration meal and recite every verse together.
Decide which book or theme comes next.
weeks.pray: Thank God for what he's done in you through James. Ask him to keep it growing.

oneLine: Real faith shows up in real life.
intro: James is short (five chapters, 108 verses) and intensely practical: about 50 commands in 108 verses. It reads like Proverbs: short punchy sections about trials, temptation, words, money, fights, plans, patience and prayer. That makes it ideal for a family learning to turn what they read into what they do.

context.p: James, a younger brother of Jesus (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19). While Jesus was teaching, his brothers didn't believe in him (John 7:5). Then the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he became the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15). Yet he introduces himself only as 'a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ'.

'The twelve tribes in the Dispersion': Jewish Christians scattered away from Jerusalem, many after persecution broke out there (Acts 8:1; 11:19). Most were poor, far from home and pushed around by rich landowners. Their church gatherings had problems: favouritism, quarrels, sharp tongues, and people who said they believed but didn't live like it.
Probably the mid-40s AD, which may make it the earliest letter in the New Testament: written within about 15 years of Jesus's death and resurrection. James was killed for his faith in AD 62.

James never quotes Jesus directly, but he echoes the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) again and again: joy in trials, asking and receiving, hearing and doing, mercy, words, treasure that rusts, yes meaning yes. James had heard his brother teach. Each week has a 'Jesus said it first' link.

checkin: Say this week's verse together from memory. Who can say it alone?
How did our 'This week we will' go? Where did we actually see it happen?
What is one thing from this passage you want to keep doing?
Read the Principles wall aloud: every principle so far.
